clue.text: Soc girl in returning train going round bend

indicators.note: going round says the reversed train word encircles the bend word
returning tells us to read the word for train from back to front

parts.note: to train a gun is to aim it
an arc is a curve or bend

explanation.surface: A society girl sits on a train that doubles back round a curve in the line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'train' looks like a railway noun but is the verb, to point a gun; 'returning' reverses it and 'going round' wraps it about the bend.
explanation.definitionFit: In S. E. Hinton's novel The Outsiders the rich kids are the Socs, and Marcia is one of the Soc girls.

clue.text: A publication written about a lizard

indicators.note: about signals turning round, so the publication word is written backwards

parts.note: a mag is a magazine

explanation.surface: A magazine runs an article about a lizard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning' in the surface, but with 'written' it reverses the publication word.
explanation.definitionFit: The agama is an Old World lizard of Africa and Asia, a genus name used as a common name.

clue.text: The—— melted from their limbs, / Nor rot nor reek did they" (Coleridge)

definitions.text: The—— melted from their limbs, / Nor rot nor reek did they" (Coleridge)

parts.words: The—— melted from their limbs, / Nor rot nor reek did they" (Coleridge)
parts.note: a gap-fill from The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, describing the dead crew lying on deck

explanation.surface: Lines from Coleridge's Rime with the phrase for the dead sailors' clammy perspiration removed.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the clammy perspiration of fear or illness on the dead sailors' skin.

clue.text: God of poetry's a flipping cut above half-cut God of mischief

indicators.note: above means set on top of, in a down entry, so these pieces come first
flipping means turning over, so the cut word is reversed

parts.note: to lop is to cut off

indicators.note: half-cut means having half its letters cut away, keeping the first half

parts.note: Loki is the Norse god of mischief

explanation.surface: A god of verse rates himself a cut above a drunken trickster god.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-cut' (British for tipsy) here leaves only LO of LOKI.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek god Apollo leads the Muses and presides over music and verse.

clue.text: Literary erotica writer of Nana is Ninety

indicators.note: of here means made out of, so the name is drawn from inside the phrase that follows

explanation.surface: It reads like a claim about Zola's Nana, the novel of a courtesan, reaching ninety.
explanation.walkthrough: The name runs across the words, from the second letter of Nana to the middle of Ninety.
explanation.definitionFit: Anaïs Nin was a French-born diarist famous for her erotic stories such as Delta of Venus.

clue.text: Headteacher is a bulbous meddler, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things going wrong, signalling the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: A sneering verdict on a portly, interfering school head.
explanation.definitionFit: Albus Dumbledore is the headmaster of Hogwarts in the Harry Potter books.

clue.text: Month after a month ignoring a spoilt sibling

indicators.note: after says this month comes at the end
a month ignoring a: the a sits in front while the month word drops its own a, so that letter shifts to the front

parts.note: May is a month
March is a month

explanation.surface: A spoilt child's birthday month falls just after another.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'a month ignoring a' as the letter a placed before a month that leaves out its own a. 'spoilt' belongs to the definition; it is not an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Amy March is the indulged youngest sister in Louisa May Alcott's Little Women.

clue.text: Way in which bed's tucked in for chap detailingNigel's fortunes

indicators.note: tucked in means slipped inside, so the bed goes inside the way

parts.note: St is short for street, a way
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: A man telling Nigel's fortunes in a room where the bed is made up.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter Scott wrote the novel The Fortunes of Nigel, set in Jacobean London.

clue.text: In which Irena comes home in new canoe with ring

indicators.note: new means made afresh, so the letters are reformed

explanation.surface: A woman paddles back home in a fresh canoe wearing a ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Milan Kundera's novel Ignorance follows the émigré Irena's return to Prague.

clue.text: Shipping magnate seen in bay up partying with model

indicators.note: partying suggests letters let loose and jumbled together, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A tycoon is spotted living it up in a bay with a fashion model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partying' rearranges BAY UP and MODEL; 'seen in' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: In Dickens's Dombey and Son the elder Paul Dombey heads a great shipping and trading house.

clue.text: Napoleon's outburst about home is fine

indicators.note: about says the word for fine goes around the word for home

parts.note: OK means fine or all right
in means at home

explanation.surface: The French emperor shouts that the house is in good order.
explanation.walkthrough: The Napoleon meant is the pig who rules in Orwell's Animal Farm, not the emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: A pig's grunt is its noise, so the outburst of Orwell's pig leader is a grunt-word.

clue.text: Prince and king with donkeys touring city

parts.note: R is short for rex, Latin for king

indicators.note: touring means travelling around, so the donkeys word goes round the city

parts.note: asses are donkeys
LA is Los Angeles

explanation.surface: A prince and a king ride donkeys on a tour of some city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince' is the definition alone; 'and' and 'with' only link the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Johnson's philosophical tale is The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia.

clue.text: Functions hosting men and Sibyl Vane's male colleagues?

indicators.note: hosting means having guests inside, so the functions word holds the men

OR, other ranks, are soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Social functions laid on for men and for the colleagues of a Wilde heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: Sibyl Vane is the young actress in Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray; the question mark marks the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Sibyl Vane performed on the stage, so the men who worked with her were stage players.

clue.text: Ring primarily galvanising really earthy Middle Earth dweller?

parts.note: a ring is shaped like the letter O

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so we take the opening letter of each of the next three words

explanation.surface: A Tolkien-style tale where a ring stirs some earthy creature of Middle-earth.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the monster is not strictly Tolkien's: it lives in the middle of the earth only loosely.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogres are giant monsters of folklore, the kind of creature found in fantasy lands like Middle-earth.

clue.text: Con upset after shot cut down a Corleone?

indicators.note: after says the reversed con word follows the shot word

parts.note: a go is a shot or try

indicators.note: upset in a down entry means turned upside down, read bottom to top

to fell is to cut down

explanation.surface: A con man is shot and gunned down, like a mafia boss.
explanation.walkthrough: The Corleones are the Mafia family of The Godfather; the question mark marks one as an example of a gangster.
explanation.definitionFit: Gangster slang, popularised by Scorsese's film, for a made man of the Mafia.

clue.text: A French hit about a lead in Scribner releases

parts.note: un is French for a

indicators.note: about says the hit word goes around the letter a

parts.note: to chin someone is to punch them on the jaw

indicators.note: the lead in a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A French bestseller, publicised by the American publisher Scribner, gets released.
explanation.walkthrough: CHIN round A gives CHAIN; S, the first letter of Scribner, follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To free something from its shackles is to let it go, a synonym for setting loose.

clue.text: Heroic crew in a Saturn go for launch

indicators.note: launch suggests sending off in a new direction, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Astronauts in a Saturn rocket get the go-ahead for lift-off.
explanation.walkthrough: The Saturn rocket points to astronauts; the answer is their Greek namesakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Jason's band of heroes who sailed the Argo in search of the Golden Fleece.

clue.text: Annie Wilkes is one in fancy furs with a pen

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or ornamented, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Stephen King's obsessive nurse dressed up in fur, pen in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: In Stephen King's Misery, Annie Wilkes is an obsessive devotee of a novelist she holds captive.

clue.text: Digit written on abridged book, King Arthur's favourite

indicators.note: written on means placed after, in an across entry, the shortened book word
abridged means shortened, so the book word loses its last letter

parts.note: a tome is a large book
the thumb is a digit of the hand

explanation.surface: An illuminated book of Arthurian legend, inscribed with someone's fingerprint.
explanation.walkthrough: Fielding's burlesque play Tom Thumb makes the tiny hero King Arthur's favourite at court.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend and in Fielding's play the thumb-sized knight is the darling of Arthur's court.

clue.text: Agnes of God's opening engineers controversy ultimately

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so we take the final letter

explanation.surface: The play Agnes of God starts with an engineered row at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Agnes of God' looks like the film title; 'of' links, and the answer completes Anne Brontë's novel title with Agnes.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Brontë's first novel is named for its governess heroine, whose surname this is.

clue.text: Beauty pageant winner raises the roof for a while

indicators.note: for a while says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A beauty queen whoops so loudly that she brings the house down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for a while' signals a short stretch borrowed from the words: the end of raises, all of the, the start of roof.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible King Ahasuerus chose Esther as queen from among the most beautiful maidens of his realm.

clue.text: He does not bend his head to hear / The Burial—— read"(Wilde)

definitions.text: He does not bend his head to hear / The Burial—— read"(Wilde)

parts.words: He does not bend his head to hear / The Burial—— read"(Wilde)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Wilde's The Ballad of Reading Gaol, where the condemned man will not hear the church's funeral service read over him

explanation.surface: Lines from Wilde's prison ballad about a hanged man with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: The Burial Office is the formal order of service for the dead in the Book of Common Prayer.

clue.text: Private undergoing a change of heart in Bury

parts.note: inner means private, kept within

explanation.surface: A soldier in the Lancashire town of Bury has a sudden change of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' looks like a soldier; it is the adjective. Bury is also a town near Manchester.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter a body is to bury it in a grave.

clue.text: Castle of vice in European legends

indicators.note: in says the vice word sits inside the other pieces

parts.note: lore is a body of traditional legends
a sin is a vice

explanation.surface: A castle of wickedness features in old European tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Elsinore is the Danish castle where Shakespeare sets Hamlet.

clue.text: Butler that man with Times passed by river

indicators.note: passed by means coming after, so the river letter goes first in this down entry

parts.note: he means that man
T stands for time, so two of them make times

explanation.surface: A manservant and his employer stroll past a river with a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butler' looks like a manservant; it is the surname of a character.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhett Butler is Scarlett's dashing husband in Gone with the Wind.

clue.text: Story of Kitty Holding heading to London

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the kitty word goes round a letter

parts.note: a pot is the kitty of money staked in a card game

indicators.note: the heading to a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: The tale of a cat called Kitty who sets off for London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' looks like a cat's name, but it is the pool of money in a card game.
explanation.definitionFit: The storyline of a novel is its sequence of events, the narrative.

clue.text: Bukowski's cheap digs perhaps pushes fool over the edge

indicators.note: over the edge means driven mad, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Living in squalid lodgings drives a hapless man to madness.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Bukowski, poet of down-and-out Los Angeles, wrote of and lived in such rooms; 'perhaps' marks an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Doss-houses offering a bed for a night at a low price; digs is British slang for lodgings.

clue.text: Singer wears frilly fabric for author in censorship trials

indicators.note: wears means has on the outside, so the fabric word goes around the singer

parts.note: lace is a delicate decorative fabric, often frilled
a wren is a songbird

explanation.surface: A singer dressed in lacy fabric stands in for a writer on trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' looks like a vocalist, but it is a songbird.
explanation.definitionFit: D. H. Lawrence's Lady Chatterley's Lover was the subject of the famous 1960 obscenity trial.

clue.text: Small row about taking penultimate of English exams

indicators.note: taking means containing, so the reversed row holds a letter
about means turned around, so the row word is read backwards

parts.note: a tier is a row of seats

indicators.note: penultimate means last but one, so we take the second-last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A minor quarrel breaks out over English examinations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns S plus TIER into REITS; 'taking' puts S, the second-last letter of English, inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Students who fail sit second attempts at examinations, which in Britain are called by this name.
